hook: Time to BUILD: a production MCP server — typed tools, exposed resources, tests, an Inspector, deployment with auth, and observability. **FastMCP makes the first 80% minutes, not weeks.**

scenes.title: FastMCP: decorators turn functions into tools
scenes.sub: The Python SDK's fast path — and the C# sibling for .NET teams
scenes.narration: The official Python SDK ships FastMCP: a decorator-driven framework where plain typed functions BECOME MCP tools — annotations become schemas, docstrings become descriptions, type hints become validation. Write a function, decorate it, run — you have a stdio server. That's genuinely the whole getting-started path, and it's why AG-06 said consume-first still leaves room for internal systems: building the custom server your org needs is no longer the hard part. For C-sharp teams, the official C-sharp SDK mirrors the model — attributes on methods, ASP.NET hosting — same protocol, your native stack. The architectural reminder: FastMCP handles the protocol plumbing; YOU still own AG-02's disciplines — good descriptions, validation, actionable errors.

scenes.title: A complete stdio server in one file
scenes.body:
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
import sqlite3

mcp = FastMCP("orders")
DB = "orders.db"   # dedicated read-only role in production!

@mcp.tool()
def search_orders(customer: str, limit: int = 5) -> list[dict]:
    """Search orders by customer name fragment.

    Use for order-history questions. Do NOT use for live inventory
    (use check_inventory). Customer is a name fragment like 'acme'.
    """
    with sqlite3.connect(DB) as con:
        rows = con.execute(
            "SELECT id, customer, total, status FROM orders "
            "WHERE customer LIKE ? LIMIT ?",
            (f"%{customer}%", limit)).fetchall()
    return [{"id": r[0], "customer": r[1],
             "total": r[2], "status": r[3]} for r in rows]

@mcp.resource("order://{order_id}")
def get_order(order_id: int) -> str:
    """Full order record as readable markdown."""
    with sqlite3.connect(DB) as con:
        row = con.execute(
            "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ?", (order_id,)).fetchone()
    if not row:
        raise ValueError(f"no order {order_id} — check the id in search_orders results")
    return format_order_markdown(row)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()   # stdio transport, local use
annot: The docstring IS the tool description — AG-02 discipline lives in the docstring, enforced by convention
Pydantic-typed signature → JSON schema; types + defaults + ranges validate before your code runs
@mcp.resource exposes DATA (read path) separately from tools (actions) — the protocol's core split
scenes.narration: Twenty-five lines, two capabilities, all the AG-02 properties present: the docstring carries the when/when-not description; type hints make limit an integer with a default; the resource raises an actionable error naming the fix path. That's the FastMCP contract — your Python signature IS the schema, and the docstring IS the documentation the model reads. Note the read-only SQL and parameterized queries — the server is the trust boundary from AG-06, so the database fences from GA-18 apply here verbatim. Run this file and any MCP host can connect over stdio. What's deliberately missing: auth, remote transport, tests, observability — the remaining three chapters.

scenes.title: Design for the reader: resources, prompts, and small surfaces
scenes.sub: Typed inputs, visible state, minimal capability sets
scenes.narration: Beyond tools, complete the primitive set. Resources: expose your data as addressable URIs — order://123, file paths, report://q3 — the host app attaches them to context deliberately; design URI schemes that mirror how users think about the data. Prompts: if users repeatedly ask the same SHAPES of questions — 'summarize this order's issues' — ship them as prompt templates, user-selected, consistent. Typed everything: Pydantic models for inputs AND outputs — structured returns become renderable tables in hosts, not walls of text. And the sizing rule from AG-02 applies verbatim: keep the server's surface small and legible — five excellent tools beat fifteen overlapping ones; group or split servers rather than bloat one. Your server's tool list is a user interface — design it like one.

items.s: URIs like order://123 or report://q3 — users and hosts navigate data the way they name it
Return models, not prose → hosts render tables/cards · errors as typed results where recoverable
5 legible tools > 15 overlapping · split servers by domain instead of bloating one

scenes.narration: One more design decision with outsized consequences: state. The 2026-07-28 spec is stateless — your server should be too; if a workflow genuinely needs state across calls — a multi-step transaction, a draft being built — pass explicit handles as arguments, AG-05's pattern: 'apply_changeset' taking the handle returned by 'prepare_changeset'. Explicit handles are visible to the model, survive load balancing, and turn invisible session bugs into reviewable arguments. Versioning belongs here too: servers evolve; keep tool signatures backward-compatible where possible, document breaking changes, and let hosts pin. A server is a published API — the consumers are models and the applications hosting them, and both read your surface literally.

scenes.title: The MCP Inspector: your server's test bench
scenes.narration: The MCP SDKs ship the Inspector — a visual tool that connects to any server and lets you poke it: list tools, read their schemas, invoke calls with editable JSON, watch requests and responses flow. Development loop: start the Inspector against your server, call each tool with realistic and hostile inputs, read the errors the model would see, fix, repeat. This closes AG-02's feedback loop empirically — you're testing the model's actual experience of your tool, not your intentions for it. Then automate: the SDK provides in-memory client connections, so pytest can drive your server end-to-end — PY-22's suite, now speaking MCP: tool discovery returns the expected schema; validation rejects bad args; error messages are actionable; happy paths return the right shapes. Test the protocol surface AND the logic.

scenes.title: pytest against a live in-process server
scenes.body:
import pytest
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client

@pytest.fixture
async def session():
    params = StdioServerParameters(command="python", args=["server.py"])
    async with stdio_client(params) as (r, w):
        async with ClientSession(r, w) as s:
            await s.initialize()
            yield s

async def test_tool_schema_is_documented(session):
    tools = await session.list_tools()
    t = next(t for t in tools.tools if t.name == "search_orders")
    assert "Do NOT use" in t.description      # AG-02 boundary present
    assert t.inputSchema["properties"]["limit"]["default"] == 5

async def test_bad_args_fail_actionably(session):
    with pytest.raises(Exception) as e:
        await session.call_tool("search_orders", {"limit": -3})
    assert "limit" in str(e.value).lower()    # actionable, names the fix

async def test_resource_roundtrip(session):
    r = await session.read_resource("order://1")
    assert "customer" in r.contents[0].text
annot: The session fixture runs the REAL server process — protocol-level, not function-level
Testing the DESCRIPTION is deliberate: schema/docs drift is how tool selection silently rots
Bad-arg tests assert the error QUALITY — the property the model depends on to self-correct
scenes.narration: Three test classes that cover the server's contract with its consumers. Schema tests pin the description discipline — the 'Do NOT use' boundary and defaults stay present as the code evolves; this is where AG-02 becomes regression-protected instead of aspirational. Failure tests verify the actionable-error property with real protocol round-trips — the assertion checks the error names the fix, because that's what the loop needs. Round-trip tests prove resources and tools return what hosts will render. Compose with PY-22's FakeProvider pattern for the LOGIC underneath — the server tests cover the protocol surface; unit tests cover the internals. And add one golden question per tool — 'what would a user ask that should route here' — as living documentation that doubles as a smoke test.

scenes.title: From stdio to service: HTTP transport, auth, logs, versions
scenes.sub: Operating a remote MCP server for real users
scenes.narration: Shipping a remote server is operating a service. Transport: FastMCP's run command switches to streamable HTTP — now it sits behind normal infrastructure: load balancers, health checks, zero-downtime deploys — the stateless spec's payoff from AG-05. Auth: real OAuth — the hardened model from the 2026-07-28 revision, or a gateway in front — remote servers without auth are public tools with your credentials. Observability: structured logs of every tool call — PY-22's discipline — plus RED metrics and tracing; remember the spec no longer carries protocol-level logging, so YOUR telemetry IS the story. Versioning: pin the spec revision you implement, track deprecations, keep the surface backward-compatible. And compatibility: negotiation means old clients will connect — decide explicitly which revisions you support.

layers.s: streamable HTTP · load-balancer friendly · health checks · stateless
OAuth per spec · or gateway in front · short-lived tokens
Per-call structured logs · RED metrics · traces · cost per call
Spec revision pinned · deprecation tracking · backward-compat surface

scenes.narration: The operational checklist, as layers. Hosting: containerize, scale horizontally, exploit statelessness — no session stickiness anywhere. Auth: use the spec's OAuth rather than bespoke headers — interop with hosts is the point of the protocol, and homegrown auth breaks it; an enterprise gateway from AG-06 can absorb this if you have one. Observability specifics for MCP: log tool name, arg hash, latency, result size, and USER — not raw args when they carry sensitive data; alert on anomalies — error-rate spikes, unusual volume — AG-07's monitoring layer is your code now. Cost: remote servers pay per call for their backends; track cost per tool call and set budgets, or one enthusiastic agent loop becomes a five-figure line item. Operated well, a remote MCP server is a small, valuable, boring service — the highest compliment infrastructure gets.

recap: FastMCP: typed functions + docstrings become tools/resources in minutes — your signature is the schema, your docstring is the model's documentation
Design small surfaces: resources for data, prompts for repeated shapes, explicit handles for state; test with the Inspector plus scripted protocol tests
Remote deployment = operating a service: streamable HTTP, spec-aligned OAuth, per-call observability, pinned revisions and deprecation tracking

quiz.q: In FastMCP, what becomes the MCP tool's description?
opts: The function's docstring — so AG-02's description discipline is written in the docstring
quiz.why: The docstring convention makes documentation unavoidable — the model reads what you wrote in the docstring, verbatim.

quiz.q: What's the recommended pattern for multi-call state under the stateless spec?
opts: Explicit handles passed as tool arguments — state visible to the model, survives load balancing
quiz.why: Stateless servers can't hold per-client state between calls — explicit handles keep state reviewable and infrastructure simple.

quiz.q: Why test that tool descriptions contain 'Do NOT use' boundaries?
opts: Description drift silently degrades model tool selection — schema tests make AG-02's discipline regression-protected
quiz.why: The description is behavior: pinning it in tests prevents well-meaning refactors from randomizing the agent's choices.

code.title: The same server, deployed: HTTP + logging + auth hook
code.body:
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
import logging, structlog

log = structlog.get_logger("mcp.orders")
mcp = FastMCP("orders")

@mcp.tool()
def search_orders(customer: str, limit: int = 5) -> list[dict]:
    """Search orders by customer name fragment … (same docstring!)"""
    log.info("tool.call", tool="search_orders",
             arg_hash=hash((customer, limit)),      # not raw args
             user=current_user_id())               # auth context from hook
    ...

# Local:   mcp.run()                          # stdio
# Remote:  mcp.run(transport="http",
#                  host="0.0.0.0", port=8080,
#                  auth=oauth_provider)       # spec-aligned OAuth
#
# Ops:  per-call logs · latency histograms · error-rate alerts ·
#       cost-per-tool dashboards · pinned spec revision in CI
annot: One code base, two transports — local stdio for dev, HTTP for production
Log arg hashes + user, never raw args — telemetry without a leak surface (AG-07)
The auth hook is where user identity enters — tools stay user-agnostic, authorization centralizes

notes:
# MCP Server Development

## FastMCP
- Decorators: typed function → tool; docstring → description; Pydantic → schema.
- C# SDK mirrors it (attributes + ASP.NET hosting).
- You still own AG-02: descriptions, validation, actionable errors.

## Design
- Resources with mental-model URIs · prompts for repeated shapes · structured outputs.
- Small surfaces: ~5 legible tools; split by domain.
- Stateless: explicit handles as arguments for multi-call state.

## Testing
- MCP Inspector: interactive poke-list-invoke loop — test the model's experience.
- Scripted: in-process sessions in pytest — schema/docs drift, failure quality, round-trips.

## Deployment
- streamable HTTP · load balancer friendly · spec-aligned OAuth (or gateway).
- Observability: per-call structured logs (hash args, log user), RED metrics, cost/call.
- Pin spec revision · track deprecations · backward-compatible surface.
